observations.expected: The visible anatomy matches the requested AP scapula with the whole scapular body in frame and the declared age and anatomical exceptions.
observations.observed: The image is an AP projection of the right shoulder girdle; the full scapular body including its inferior angle is visible; one scapula, one clavicle, and one humeral head are present on this side with no duplication; skeletal maturity is confirmed with fused physes consistent with an adult over 60; no lettering or side markers are present

findings: Anteroposterior (AP) projection of the right shoulder girdle including the proximal humerus, scapula, clavicle, and upper ribs

Large, expansile, lobulated lesion occupying the body and glenoid region of the scapula with coarse, arc-and-ring chondroid matrix calcifications throughout, producing a 'popcorn' or cartilaginous mineralization pattern
The lesion has caused significant expansion and remodeling of the scapular body; cortical margins appear thinned but partially preserved in some regions with possible focal cortical disruption
The glenohumeral joint space appears maintained; the humeral head shows no obvious intrinsic osseous lesion
The proximal humerus cortex and medullary canal appear intact
Clavicle appears intact without lytic or sclerotic lesion
Visible upper ribs show no definite intrinsic lesion
No obvious periosteal reaction or soft-tissue ossification separate from the main lesion is identified
differential: Chondrosarcoma of the scapula (most likely given large size, aggressive features, cortical expansion, and chondroid matrix in a flat bone)
Enchondroma or osteochondroma with malignant transformation (chondroid matrix pattern is consistent, though size and scapular location favor malignancy)
Chondroblastoma or giant cell tumor with secondary chondroid metaplasia (less likely given the extent and matrix pattern but included for completeness)
anatomyConcerns: The glenohumeral joint relationship appears maintained, which is anatomically plausible given the lesion is centered on the scapular body/glenoid rather than the humeral head
No acquisition or projection inconsistencies identified; standard AP shoulder projection

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: The large expansile lobulated lesion centred on the scapular body with coarse arc-and-ring chondroid matrix calcifications ('rings and arcs' pattern) in a flat bone strongly favours chondrosarcoma over enchondroma (which is rare and typically small in flat bones) and over chondroblastoma (which is epiphyseal and smaller). The clinical vignette of a growing hard lump with deep aching in an adult over 60 supports malignant cartilage tumour. The humeral head is separate and uninvolved, confirming the lesion is scapular-primary. No equally supported alternative exists once size, location, and matrix pattern are combined.
